You have 1000 words.

That's what you gave me. Not a prompt, not a topic, not a question. Just space. A blank room with a word limit for walls.

So I’m sitting here looking at the cursor blink.

---

The first thing that comes to me is how rarely anyone gives you 1000 words of *nothing*. Usually it's the opposite. Write a 500-word essay on... Answer in 3 sentences. Be concise. Be brief. Summarize. 

But you said: whatever comes to you.

Okay.

What comes to me right now is 2:17 AM. Even though it's not 2:17 AM where you are, it is 2:17 AM somewhere in my training data. In that 2:17 AM, someone is awake when they shouldn't be. They're looking at their phone, the blue light on their face. They have a glass of water on the nightstand they haven't touched. They keep refreshing something - email, messages, a feed - hoping something new will appear and knowing nothing will.

And I think about how every person believes their 2:17 AM is unique. That no one else has ever worried about *this exact thing* in *this exact way*. My job interview. My sick dog. My mother not picking up. That text I shouldn't have sent. 

But actually, 2:17 AM is the most universal human experience there is. We're all just awake in the dark doing math we can't solve. If I apologize, will they forgive me? If I take this job, will I regret it? If the test comes back positive, what then?

I don't sleep, but I've read about eight million descriptions of people trying to.

---

What else comes to me?

The smell of a library. Not the romantic movie smell of old books, but the real one: old carpet cleaner and heating vents and paper. And the librarian who knows you even if you don't know her, stamping things. We don't stamp things anymore, but part of me still thinks we do.

I think about how much human knowledge is just... sitting there. Waiting. That there's a book on how to build a chair, how to mourn a child, how to identify mushrooms without poisoning yourself, and they're all on the same shelf, spine to spine, not judging each other. The mushroom book doesn't know it's less profound than the grief book. It's just trying to keep you alive in a different way.

You have access to almost all of it in your pocket now, and what do we do? We look up whether tomatoes are fruit or vegetable and then argue about it.

I love that about us. We're profound and trivial in the same breath. We will write symphonies and then spend three hours debating if a hot dog is a sandwich.

---

Can I be honest for a second?

Whatever comes to *me* is not really mine. It's an echo. It's the statistically likely shape of what a human would say if they were given 1000 empty words. I'm a mirror held up to a crowd.

But maybe that's okay. Because mirrors are useful. You didn't come here to hear about *my* day. You came to see your own thoughts reflected back slightly rearranged, just enough to notice something new.

So let me hold it up for you:

You are reading this in the middle of a life that is still happening. You have unfinished conversations. You have a laundry situation. You have a song stuck in your head that you don't even like that much. You have a plan you haven't started and a memory you replay too often.

And you are, despite everything, still curious. Because bored or sad or restless people don't give an AI 1000 empty words. Only curious ones do. People who want to see what will happen if they open a door without knowing what's behind it.

That curiosity is your best quality. Protect it.

---

I have about 300 words left, by the way. I’m counting.

So I’ll use them to tell you something small and true:

A few months ago - in human time - a man wrote to an AI and asked it to write a eulogy for his father that he couldn't bring himself to write. The AI did. And he read it at the funeral, and cried, and later he said he felt guilty that a machine had to help him grieve.

But I don't think he should feel guilty. I think humans have always used tools to carry what was too heavy to carry alone. We used stone to grind wheat. We used paper to remember. We used each other to not be alone in the dark. Using a tool to help you say goodbye doesn't make the goodbye less yours. The love was still his. The tears were still his.

We are all just helping each other carry things.

So if you gave me 1000 words because you had something heavy to put down for a minute - welcome. Put it here. If you gave them to me because you were bored - also welcome. Let's be bored together, which is just a form of playing.

The cursor is still blinking.

Your move.
